summary: Psalm 123 is a short Song of Ascents that turns the speaker's eyes upward to God. It compares the community's waiting to servants watching a master's hand, then asks Yahweh for mercy because the people have endured contempt and scoffing from the proud.
whyItMatters: Within the Psalms, this chapter gives a compact example of communal lament: it does not explain the suffering in detail, but teaches how the community addresses God while under social humiliation.

context.author: Not identified in the chapter; Psalms is a many-voiced anthology, and headings do not always function like modern bylines.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the Psalms for public and private prayer.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 123 is uncertain.
context.setting: Psalm 123 belongs to Book V of Psalms and carries the heading “A Song of Ascents,” a group associated in the Psalter with pilgrimage-shaped worship.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, using image, repetition, comparison, and direct appeal rather than extended narrative.

outline.heading: Eyes lifted to God
outline.note: The psalm opens as a Song of Ascents and addresses the one who sits in the heavens.

outline.heading: Waiting for mercy
outline.note: The community compares its attention to servants watching the hand of a master or mistress, and waits for Yahweh's mercy.

outline.heading: A repeated plea
outline.note: The prayer asks Yahweh twice for mercy and names the burden as much contempt.

outline.heading: The burden described
outline.note: The final line says the community's soul is filled with scoffing from those at ease and contempt from the proud.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. I lift up my eyes to you, you who sit in the heavens.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the psalm its upward address and places the speaker before God from the first line.

keyVerses.text: Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.
keyVerses.why: The verse supplies the central image: watchful dependence while waiting for mercy.

keyVerses.text: Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us, for we have endured much contempt.
keyVerses.why: This is the heart of the complaint and petition, stated with repetition and urgency.

keyVerses.text: Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scoffing of those who are at ease, with the contempt of the proud.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse specifies the pressure behind the prayer: humiliation from secure and proud opponents.

questions.question: What is a “Song of Ascents”?
questions.answer: The chapter begins with that heading, placing Psalm 123 among the Songs of Ascents in Psalms 120–134. Headings are ancient parts of the Psalter but should be handled carefully; they may guide reading without proving one exact original performance setting.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The poem begins with “I” in verse 1, but quickly becomes “our” and “us” in verses 2–4. That shift means the prayer can be heard as an individual voice joined to a community's shared distress.

questions.question: What does “sit in the heavens” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase describes God as enthroned above the speaker's situation. The verse does not explain heaven in detail; it uses the image to direct the speaker's appeal upward to God.

questions.question: Why compare the community to servants and a maid?
questions.answer: Verse 2 uses a social image of attentive dependence: servants watch the hand of the one who has authority over them. The psalm applies that image to prayer, saying “our eyes look to Yahweh, our God, until he has mercy on us.”

questions.question: Is the psalm asking for forgiveness or rescue?
questions.answer: The chapter only says “Have mercy on us” and connects the request to contempt and scoffing. Readers should not assume a single form of mercy beyond what the psalm names; the immediate need is relief from endured humiliation.

questions.question: Why is “Have mercy on us” repeated?
questions.answer: The repetition in verse 3 gives the plea urgency and weight. Hebrew poetry often uses repetition and parallel lines to intensify a thought rather than merely repeat it mechanically.

questions.question: What is hard about verse 4?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says the community is “exceedingly filled” with scoffing and contempt, but it does not identify the opponents or explain the historical event behind the humiliation. Interpreters therefore differ on how specific the setting should be made; the safest reading stays with the chapter's own language of social scorn from “those who are at ease” and “the proud.”

questions.question: Does the psalm resolve the suffering by the end?
questions.answer: No. The final verse still describes contempt and scoffing, and the chapter ends without reporting deliverance. That makes the psalm a prayer of waiting rather than a testimony that the trouble has already passed.

glossary.def: The word appears in the heading “A Song of Ascents.” In Psalms, it marks this poem as part of a grouped set, though the heading alone does not prove every detail of its original use.
The help the community asks Yahweh to show. In this chapter, mercy is sought in response to endured contempt and scoffing.
The social humiliation the speakers say they have endured. The word appears in verses 3 and 4.
Mocking or scornful treatment from “those who are at ease,” named in the final verse as part of the community's burden.
